item.title: Escaping the Osho Cult
item.description:
Conformity

Escaping the Osho Cult

Psychotherapist and cult survivor Nicola Ranson recalls escaping a violent cult.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional and psychological vulnerabilities often make people susceptible to influence from cult leaders.
  • Life changes, lack of family support, and attraction to charismatic leaders are common reasons people join.
  • The influence of a cult can last long after the person has left the cult community.
  • Many survivors find support from therapy, other survivors, and friends outside of the influence of the cult.

We can learn a lot about social psychological persuasion from talking to cult survivors. I recently had the privilege of interviewing psychotherapist, educator, and cult survivor Nicola Ranson. Her memoir, A Slice of Orange: Loving and Leaving the Osho/Rajneesh Cult (Unsolicited Press, Dec. 2026), vividly reveals how bright people can fall victim to toxic psychosocial manipulation. With a strong resonant voice and warm British accent, Ranson shares some hard-won wisdom in the following discussion:

Source: Photo by Ken Kebow

Gina Simmonds Schneider: What first inspired you to join the Rajneesh Movement?

Nicola Ranson: Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, now known as Osho, was an Indian guru who moved his ashram from India to Oregon in the 1980s. He was formerly a philosophy professor and lectured extensively on a wide range of religions. I was drawn to his eclectic teachings, which combined Western psychotherapy and Eastern mysticism. I went to India in 1979 and participated in the mandatory therapy groups inspired by the Human Potential Movement—popular at that time. Rajneesh’s groups (and meditations) included cathartic practices which are now almost obsolete in psychotherapy due to the harm they can cause.

In Oregon, we constructed a city on a vast 100-square-mile tract of land. It housed over 4,000 permanent residents and over 30,000 temporary festival visitors. The movement there fell apart after a grand jury investigation found the leadership guilty of multiple crimes, including poisoning over 750 people in the Dalles in an attempt to sway an election. That earned the cult the dubious distinction of causing the largest bioterrorist attack in modern American history. The Oregon commune folded in 1985, but the group continues to this day with a headquarters in India.

I joined when I was 24. The guru’s teachings met my desire for personal growth and fascination with spirituality. I shared his interest in multiple religions and liked that he encouraged me to trust my own experience. He told us not to elevate him, that he was simply a doorway to the divine. He was handsome and charismatic, and I was drawn to him. It felt like a calling. Plus, he'd amassed an extraordinary international community surrounding him. In retrospect, that vibrant group played a larger role in the appeal than I realized at the time.

GSS: Research shows that social, psychological, or emotional vulnerabilities can make one more susceptible to cult programming (Rousselet, et al. 2017). What made you vulnerable?

NR: It's true that while cults can attract anyone, certain circumstances make us more vulnerable and one of those is life transitions. I was at a crossroads. I’d finished university, and most of my friends had moved on. I had just botched an important job interview and lacked family support. I was awed by the disciples I met who seemed so happy and fulfilled, and I wanted to know their secret.

GSS: The social influence of a cult community can keep people feeling trapped inside, even when they know something is wrong (Hassan, 2015). When did you first realize something was wrong?

NR: From the initial attraction to declaring that I was fully done—and naming it a cult—was ten years of my life. Yes, there were a number of times when I sensed something was wrong and ignored my inner guidance. I had been conditioned not to trust my own mind. We were taught not to be “negative” and to see discomfort as a sign that our ego was being challenged. But absolutely there were times when I knew something was wrong and recognized that I was afraid to speak up publicly.

I discussed this with trusted friends, but my mind did calisthenics with the cognitive dissonance that arose. I had to face that the community I believed was based on love and bettering the planet had committed cruel and criminal actions. It was difficult to determine who was responsible for the crimes. There was a lot of blame and deflection going on that didn’t ring true to me. When the Oregon commune fell apart, I was in shell shock and had to figure out how to restart my life at thirty with no money and no résumé.

I was homeless on the beach when I arrived in San Diego, and my fellow disciples were still family to me. Some were willing to question the guru, but many were not. Complete extrication took years—and is a process that continues. Look at how long it can take someone to get out of a bad romantic relationship. My relationship was not only with a guru but with an entire community, many of whom remain close friends.

GSS: Many cult survivors describe feeling shattered and broken after leaving a cult (Hadding et al., 2023). How did you eventually leave? What helped you recover?

NR: When I saw the discrepancy between what the group proclaimed and the unkind and unethical behavior taking place, something inside me broke, and I began to question everything. When the commune folded, we were all asked to leave, but my mental extrication took longer. We had been told that outsiders were hostile and couldn’t possibly understand spiritual truth, which of course made us feel special and created a sense of “us” and “them.” I hadn’t left the commune in four years, but when I got out and began making friends outside, I realized it was arrogant, self-serving nonsense.

I think my friendships, both with other cult members who were open to questioning and with kind people who accepted me and my past, were the most helpful components of recovery. When I studied social work and group and organizational dynamics, I learned a lot about social influence and how groups behave (which led me to teach group behavior in National University’s counseling psychology department for seventeen years).

As a psychotherapist, I learned a lot from my clients when I saw cult dynamics play out in abusive relationships, sometimes known as cults of one. We need more education to inoculate the general population from the trap of toxic cults. Undue influence and coercive control can show up in multiple areas of our society, including work, healthcare, religion, and politics. We need more resources to help survivors recover and to better understand the cultic influences that can impact any of us.

item.title: How to Get Out of Feeling Lonely
item.description:
Loneliness

How to Get Out of Feeling Lonely

See how attachment theory provides a roadmap for overcoming loneliness.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness can be triggered by present events, but it often has its roots in earlier life experiences.
  • Attachment patterns help explain why some people feel lonely even when surrounded by others.
  • Healing unresolved emotional wounds can reduce feelings of loneliness in adulthood.
  • Learning to validate others and provide a secure base can help them feel less alone.
Source: Ground Picture/Shutterstock

The fact that people are lonely isn’t new, despite the U.S. Surgeon General proclaiming in 2023 that loneliness and isolation are a national epidemic. People have always been lonely, even when they are surrounded by people. If you are old enough, you might remember a line from the Beatles' 1966 song Eleanor Rigby: "... All the lonely people... Where do they all come from?"

You might be one of those lonely people. Or you might be struggling to understand someone you are in a relationship with. In either case, this article should help by giving you concrete ideas about what you can do.

Loneliness as a Product of Attachment Styles

Attachment styles are personality characteristics that develop in childhood and provide us with roadmaps for understanding and navigating the social world as adults. There are four basic attachment styles.

Secure. If our early family relationships were with parents who were consistently warm, available, and responsive, we probably would have developed a secure attachment style. In this case, your parents would have been emotionally perceptive and understanding of your emotional needs. If you were upset or frightened, they would have 1) accurately perceived your experience, 2) shown you in their words and facial expressions that they understood what you were experiencing, and then, after having validated your perceptions and joined you in your emotional experiences, they may have 3) attempted to comfort you or given you another way of looking at things. In this context, you would not have felt alone in your struggles. By extension, relative to those with insecure attachment styles, people with secure styles are the least likely to feel lonely in adulthood (Shorter et al., 2022).

Avoidant/Dismissing. If your parents took the approach that children should not be coddled, they may have let you face your struggles alone. They probably would not have perceived your experience accurately or recognized when you were hurt or upset. By extension, they would not have reflected your experience in their words or in their facial expressions. You would have been alone with your emotions and would not have known what to do with them. Instead of learning to sit with your difficult feelings, you would have buried them away, refused to look at them, and denied to yourself and others that anything was wrong. As an adult, you would continue to repress your lonely feelings. But underneath the facade you would still have a deeper sense of being alone.

Anxious/Preoccupied. If your parents were inconsistent, sometimes warm and accepting, sometimes cold or rejecting, you may have learned to distrust whether people would be there for you when you needed them. Your parents will have supported and validated you often enough that you would always keep reaching out for them and trying, but it would expose you to continuing to be periodically misread and invalidated. You will have kept trying anyway, continued to have strong emotions, and stayed vigilant for threat cues and signs of rejection. So, if you felt lonely in childhood, you may have felt it intensely and repeatedly and may have tried to cling to others out of a sense of desperation. Even if you had a romantic partner or best friend, you would never fully trust that they weren’t going to leave you alone.

Fearful (Anxious and Avoidant). If your parents were frightened or frightening, you may have learned early on that those who were supposed to have loved you hurt you. In this case, you may never have experienced someone else mirroring you accurately or seeing your perspective. You may have developed a sense of aloneness early in life that never went away even if you were able to hide from it for periods of time. In adulthood, you may have a chronic sense of loneliness that never goes away even when you are surrounded by people or have a romantic partner.

Loneliness as Emotional Memory

Sometimes emotions like loneliness are not caused by current events. Rather, things in the current environment, including people, can trigger an emotional experience that was already in you. These emotional memories would have come from childhood experiences with parents and later from friends and romantic partners. Adolescence, for example, was a confusing and lonely time for many people. Because of the confusion, strong emotions from painful social experiences may have been stored separately from the events that originally created them. When an adult event is similar enough to the original event, it may trigger the emotional experience without you recalling the original incident… So, it seems that the emotion is coming from what just happened in adulthood even if the origin was actually decades earlier.

So, if you feel lonely….

Take a look at yourself first. Is the feeling familiar? If something happened to make you feel lonely, see if you can view it as a triggering event of an emotion that already had a place in your experience. Then see if you can sit with the feeling in your body without trying to make it go away, and attach it to a memory from earlier in your life. Go back as far as you can. If you can heal that original wound or period of your life, you may find that your loneliness in adulthood becomes much less intense. (Click here for understanding inner child work and here for how to shift your emotional memories).

Increase your social support. Don’t rely on one or two people for all your social needs. Most adults will eventually get tired of this and let you down. Try to branch out and join activity-based groups, clubs, or volunteer organizations or find a local (in person!) self-help group.

See if you are protecting yourself. Sometimes when we are afraid of getting hurt or rejected, we will cut ourselves off from others before they get the chance. In this case, we may not feel rejected, but we will certainly feel isolated and alone.

Ask for the validation you need. You aren’t responsible for other people’s actions, but don’t assume that your relationship partners realize that they are doing something to contribute to your loneliness. From their own attachment style lens, especially if they are avoidant, they might not be doing anything wrong. But you can coach them to respond to you in ways that help you feel understood, supported, and less alone.

Remember the pattern that secure parents use when their children are upset:

1. Perceive the other person’s feelings and experience.

2. Mirror their experience through your voice, facial expressions, and body language.

3. Validate their feelings and experience. This is where you verbally acknowledge that the other person has a right to their perspective and experience… without you changing it or making them wrong.

4. Hold the other person’s emotions and perspectives. This means you join them in their experience at least for a short time. Sit with them in their sadness, anger, or fear without trying to change it.

5. Upregulate. This is where you begin gently lifting the other person's emotional state. After they feel understood and validated, you can gradually introduce a different perspective or positive emotion. Notice that you are not arguing with their experience or telling them they shouldn't feel the way they do. Instead, you are helping them move toward a more hopeful emotional state while still honoring what they are feeling.

6. Recheck. Check in on how the other person is feeling and, if possible, let them know you continue to be available to them.

If you skip the steps and go directly to upregulating, you will have ignored and invalidated the other person’s perspective and feelings and tried to replace them with your own perspective and how you want them to feel. If you do this, the other person will feel:

Alone with their thoughts.

Alone with their feelings.

Alone with their struggles.

Alone... and lonely.

item.title: Sibling Estrangement Is Seldom an Impulsive Decision
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Sibling Estrangement Is Seldom an Impulsive Decision

What pushes adult siblings apart?

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Sibling estrangement is not as rare as people might think.
  • Seldom is estrangement an impulsive decision—it's often a "last-resort" effort at self-protection.
  • Early family dynamics can drive later-life estrangement between siblings.
  • Perhaps surprisingly, grief and relief often coexist for those who initiate estrangement.

Sibling relationships are usually the ones that last the longest of any relationships in our lives. In many families, siblings enter each other’s lives before memory fully develops; they often remain throughout older adulthood; and we share a family history that others might not understand (Gilligan et al., 2020). Siblings know our strengths and weaknesses, and that can be a boon or a burden as we mature.

It’s also key to recognize that sibling estrangement is not as rare as many think. Hank and Steinbach (2023) found that around 28 percent of individuals in their large-scale family study, with 10,000 sibling dyads, had experienced estrangement with a sibling. They also found that sibling estrangement was often temporary and more likely in situations where significant family transitions were more frequent.

People often assume that estrangement is impulsive or selfish, but it generally comes as a last resort after years of trying to reshape a relationship. In fact, the stories of individuals in my qualitative study of estrangement underscore the truth that their decision was made after longstanding efforts of trying to maintain or reshape a dysfunctional relationship. After years of failed efforts, they finally decided that distance was the healthiest choice for them to make. While estrangement is a clear endpoint to dealing with relationships that lack safety, trust, and potential for change, there are many pathways that lead individuals to this decision.

The Accumulation of Hurt

When we think about how people develop over time, we know that much of our development is cumulative, meaning it builds over time. We learn about relationships this way, as well, and the accumulation of painful relational experiences builds up over time through repeated interactions. Eventually, though, we comprehend the limits of the relationship to satisfy our needs, and we reach the tipping point of estrangement or continued engagement.

Sibling relationships can have an interesting dynamic due to their involuntary-voluntary nature. As children, there is no escaping family bonds, but with adulthood, continued relationships with siblings become more of a choice. In some families that have been sites of abuse, trauma bonding between siblings can occur, which can complicate adult sibling relationships in unexpected ways that lead to conflict or estrangement. In seemingly “happy families,” rivalry or resentment can fester for years and then manifest as estrangement in adulthood.

Pain Can Arise From So Many Circumstances

In some families, other dynamics are at play that may begin in childhood and have lasting, and often intensifying, influence on the sibling relationship into adulthood. These include parental favoritism, scapegoating of one sibling, “golden child” dynamics in which one child can do no wrong, and parental enabling of poor behavior. As people shared about their decision to estrange a sibling, the relationship with the sibling could not easily be separated from the larger family system in which the relationship developed, in many cases. As one woman observed, “I can identify the patterns that exist in this toxic relationship with this sibling [as] really a reflection of how my overall family dynamic created this toxicity. So, it really reveals a bigger picture.”

While many of the individuals who shared their stories pointed to a “last straw,” they affirmed it marked the culmination of years of hurt caused by their sibling. The pain described had been inflicted through a variety of means, including verbal assault, manipulation, criticism, and betrayal.

An example of verbal attacks and criticism, a woman shared, “My brother was verbally abusing me and falsely calling me an ‘inheritance whore’ for maintaining contact and care for my mom who cut him out of her will after he estranged himself from her. The goal: protect my mental health and peace of mind.” Another person described betrayal by their brother, “My brother was my business partner, and he went behind my back and colluded with others and created a huge financial loss for me and my family.” These were examples of the final straw, when a person had endured the situation as long as they could.

One of the strongest themes shared was the presence of abuse by a sibling. Abuse can take many forms, including emotional abuse, verbal abuse, and sexual abuse. One woman in her 50s shared her reason for estrangement from a sister, “I didn’t want to be a part of her drama or manipulation anymore. She was 12 years older than me and sexually abused me when I was 5 years old. I repressed those memories until I couldn’t anymore.” Bullying and intimidation, in childhood and adulthood, are other behaviors that led to estrangement.

It’s More Than a Single Incident

Regardless of the relationship, estrangement is rarely about a single incident between two people. It typically reflects longstanding emotional wounds that haven’t healed; persistent conflict that cannot be settled; chronic disrespect or denigration; or feelings of being unseen or unvalued.

"Estrangement was not what I wanted, but what I wanted was not going to happen."
— Initiator of Sibling Estrangement, in her 60s

For some participants, estrangement represented an act of self-preservation rather than rejection. After having spent a lifetime defending against a sibling’s attacks, they reached a point where they would not tolerate being harmed any longer. When interactions consistently feel unsafe or damaging, the expectation of lifelong family loyalty may begin to lose its meaning.

What the initiators were striving to do through their decisions to enact distance with their siblings was to meet very basic needs. A striking number of participants used the language of survival, relief, and peace when describing life after estrangement. They shared goals of reducing anxiety, protecting emotional well-being, ending chronic stress, and creating peace for themselves and their families-of-creation.

Grief and Relief Often Co-Exist

"It has been a sense of relief on one hand... On the other hand, I mourn for the family I wish they were."
— Initiator of Sibling Estrangement, in his 60s

Perhaps the most poignant revelations from these narratives described the combination of relief and grief that initiators were left carrying. They grieved the relationship that they could have had with their sibling but recognized that letting it go was the only clear path to the relief they needed. Estrangement is often a painful acknowledgment that a relationship that should have been cherished has become too damaging to sustain.

item.title: Rest in Peace, Dr. Gordon G. Gallup, Jr.
item.description:
Evolutionary Psychology

Rest in Peace, Dr. Gordon G. Gallup, Jr.

A tribute to a one-of-a-kind behavioral scientist.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Gordon Gallup, who recently passed away, was a true icon of behavioral science.
  • Gordon shed groundbreaking light on self-awareness, fight-or-flight response, mating, and much more.
  • The world truly lost one of the greats. Gordon Gallup was one-of-a-kind and he will be sorely missed.
The author, Glenn Geher, with Gordon Gallup
Source: Nate Pipitone

It hurts me to write that my dear friend (and dear friend to many), Dr. Gordon Gallup, has passed away. Gordon’s influence on the field of evolutionary behavioral science has been both multi-faceted and profound. Gordon was gentle, kind, caring, brilliant, and wildly creative. He had a beautiful mind and soul. And he will be deeply missed by so many.

To say that Gordon Gallup, a world-renowned behavioral scientist at SUNY Albany for most of his career, had an enormous impact would be an understatement. At the proximate level, Gordon was known for his generosity; he would give the shirt off his back for those whom he cared about. He had a reputation as a family man—a devoted husband, father, and grandfather. And anyone fortunate to call him a friend knew him to be a friend in the most genuine sense. Despite an extraordinary workload, he would always pause to talk with you. He would always take time to help you advance your ideas; he would do what he could to help you with pretty much anything.

As a professor, he took a uniquely caring, other-oriented approach to his work. Unlike so many other elite researchers, he obviously and truly cared about teaching and about his students. He cared about his many graduate students over the years, a group of bright scholars who now hold many academic positions—these alumni light up upon hearing or speaking his name. Many alumni describe his influence as life-changing and like nothing I’ve ever seen. He actually cared. He stands as the greatest academic mentor I’ve ever known. As a scholar, he was world-class. Despite having a deeply down-to-earth manner, Gordon was an influential research scholar.

His work covered a broad array of topics: the fight-or-flight response in various vertebrates, self-awareness in non-human primates, learned taste aversion across species, the evolutionary psychology of human mating and relationships, biochemical and morphological facets of human mating and relationships, behavioral features of human intimate relationships, handgrip strength as a core feature of primate life, and much more. Gordon, with a background in primatology, comparative psychology, and animal behavior, had a unique capacity to use evolutionary principles to shed new light on so many facets of the living world. It is no wonder that he was asked at one point to serve as the keynote speaker for the American Psychological Association–one of the greatest honors that can be bestowed upon anyone in the field.

When I started teaching at SUNY New Paltz, an hour from Albany, I was eager to advance my teaching and research in evolutionary psychology. People from all different places started to tell me that I must get to know Gordon Gallup. Sure, I’d heard of this legendary scholar, but it was hard for me to understand why so many people saw my meeting with him as an imperative.

That is, until I actually met him, a game-changing moment in my career and in my life.

Before meeting Gordon in person, I emailed him about forming a regional intellectual society dedicated to advancing evolutionary psychology. We would hold annual conferences in the Northeast. Our first conference was set for April 2007–and Gordon had graciously agreed to serve as a keynote speaker. With this fact alone, there was reason for optimism about the Northeastern Evolutionary Psychology Society.

When Gordon showed up at the conference on my home campus of SUNY New Paltz, I immediately saw why Gordon’s reputation so emphatically preceded him. He was wearing worn-out jeans, a black t-shirt, and a well-worn flannel. He looked like he had just come from the fields (it wasn’t surprising when I learned that he lived on a working cattle farm). He had the most genuine and kind smile and demeanor. And he spoke in a way that was uniquely engaging and welcoming. And he literally had a twinkle in his eyes at all times.

I thought: Yes, this guy is so the real deal, just like people had told me. Gordon was that rare kind of person who you just got to know almost immediately. Gordon attended that first conference in its entirety. He brought a dozen undergraduate and graduate students, ensuring that attendance for the first conference would be solid, an essential ingredient for launching an intellectual society. He interacted with other attendees as if he was at a family reunion. I think what stood out most to me was his authentically egalitarian manner of interaction. He would spend just as much time and interest in talking with a freshman who was halfway through an introductory psychology course as he would talking to a highly published peer from an Ivy League institution.

My admiration for Gordon was immediate. For years, we stayed in touch. We would visit one another’s campuses regularly, usually bringing students to create an informal Albany-New Paltz evolutionary psychology community. Gordon contributed some of the most important chapters to multiple books that I co-edited. Each time he visited New Paltz was like a visit from a cherished family member. And hearing him talk about his research and ideas was always delightful, provocative, and engaging. No one fell asleep during a lecture by Gordon Gallup. No one.

Everyone who knew Gordon well could drop multiple anecdotes—stories of insightful learning moments, among other things. Listening to him dissect his ideas was like seeing the world illuminated for the first time. I will never forget one occasion when he was giving a lecture to students and faculty on my campus. He was talking about his research on handgrip strength. At some point, he paused for questions. I raised my hand and asked him this: Can you please briefly summarize why handgrip strength is so important from an evolutionary perspective, in the first place? As was usually the case when Gordon answered questions of this variety, his answer was delivered with lightning speed and razor-sharp clarity: We need to keep in mind that for millions of generations in the evolutionary history of our lineage, our ancestors were arboreal tree-dwellers. And if you live primarily in the treetops—and you fail to grab a branch on any single occasion, it’s lights out. To deeply understand the point, that was all I needed to hear. I tell this anecdote to students every semester since.

The uniquely brilliant mind and generous nature of Gordon Gallup, Jr. greatly influenced my career. But more importantly, I learned from Gordon what it means to be a good man. And I know that countless others feel the same way. Gordon’s influence on our world, at so many levels, has been both positive and, to use one of Gordon’s favorite words, ubiquitous.

Rest in peace, Gordon. Thanks for the gift of the Northeastern Evolutionary Psychology Society. Thanks for all you did to make this world a better place. You will always be loved.

item.title: Toward a More Empathic Measure of Pain
item.description:
Chronic Pain

Toward a More Empathic Measure of Pain

Pain may not be purely private in the way we once assumed.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • A new brainwave-based system classifies pain levels while reducing the bias of self-reported pain scores.
  • It trains on the most useful and reliable examples, rather than treating every report as equally trustworthy.
  • The findings suggest that pain intensity may leave measurable traces in brain activity.

How do we know what another person feels? This question sits at the center of medicine, philosophy, and ordinary human life. We can see another person wince or laugh, and listen when they describe joy, sadness, fear, or pain. Still, their inner world remains partly hidden.

For physicians, understanding and managing pain is one of the hardest parts of caring for patients. Pain reports guide medication, surgery, recovery plans, and comfort at the bedside. But self-reported pain has a fragile foundation. Two people can receive the same stimulus and give very different answers to their pain level.

A recent study presents a system that uses electroencephalography, a method for recording brainwaves, to classify pain intensity and provide a more objective lens into another person’s suffering. In doing so, it joins a broader series of studies asking whether subjective states, including pain, can be measured in quantifiable biological signals.

Listening to Pain

The study involved participants who received controlled painful stimulation, rated their perceived pain intensity on a numerical scale, and had their brain activity recorded. The proposed system uses two matching machine learning models that learn side by side. Each model examines the same brainwave sample and tries to classify its pain level. During training, the system asks two questions about each example.

First, does the reported pain score seem reliable? If the brainwave pattern strongly conflicts with the reported label, the example receives less trust. Second, does the example teach the model something useful? If the two models disagree, the sample may sit near a boundary between pain levels and help sharpen the system’s judgment.

The system then ranks the examples. It gives priority to samples that appear trustworthy while still carrying useful information. As training continues, it gradually leaves out examples that look unreliable or unhelpful. In this way, the machine learns while filtering some of the noise inside subjective reports.

The Brain’s Signature of Suffering

The study also looked for brain regions and rhythms linked to pain prediction. The strongest signals appeared near brain regions involved in attention, emotion, and the interpretation of bodily experience. The brain judges threat, remembers past injury, predicts danger, and directs attention toward the body.

The study points toward future tools for patients who cannot clearly describe pain. This includes people with impaired consciousness, advanced dementia, severe neurological disease, or communication barriers. In such settings, clinicians often must infer pain. Brainwave-based systems could one day add another source of evidence for these situations. For the first time, such approaches raise the possibility of an external, brain-based estimate of pain intensity, rather than relying only on what a patient can say or how a clinician interprets their behavior.

Pain as a Message

Understanding another person’s internal feelings is a general human problem. Joy, sadness, fear, fatigue, anxiety, and suffering all depend on subjective experience. Medicine often turns these experiences into scores, scales, and categories, but those labels are imperfect translations of inner life.

Yet pain may not be purely private in the way we once assumed, and may leave measurable traces in the brain that correspond, at least partly, to internal perception. A growing series of studies is beginning to ask whether such internal states can be measured more directly.

The answer is still incomplete. We cannot yet know another person’s qualia, the raw feel of their experience, with full certainty. We cannot prove that your green looks like my green, or that your pain carries the same emotional impact as mine. But studies like this suggest that the boundary between private experience and measurable biology may be more porous than previously thought.

If used carefully, these new technologies could deepen rather than diminish empathy. They could help clinicians understand patients more precisely, treat pain more fairly, and come closer to one of medicine’s oldest goals: understanding what another person feels.

item.title: Dial Down Anxiety With Evolution
item.description:
Anxiety

Dial Down Anxiety With Evolution

Evolution made us overanxious, but we can do something about it.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Our bodies sometimes overreact to stressors as if they were lethal, when they're not.
  • Such extreme anxiety stems from evolution favoring brains that overreacted versus under-reacted to threats.
  • Understanding how the brain unconsciously makes you overanxious with outdated reasoning can ease anxiety.

A scenario provoking extreme anxiety

Brad knew something was wrong the moment his boss entered the conference room for the weekly staff meeting. Normally cheerful and energetic, the boss moved sluggishly, his face haggard. He slumped into his chair, cleared his throat, and delivered the bad news: their entire department was being eliminated as part of a corporate merger.

Back at his desk after the meeting, Brad stared numbly at the wall of his cubicle, seeing only a bleak future without a salary or health insurance. How would he pay for the mortgage, the kid’s private school? Getting a new job as a programmer in the age of AI would be monumentally difficult. A dark voice in his head screamed: Your life is over. A growing panic seized Brad. His muscles tensed, his heart pounded, his stomach twisted, and breathing grew rapid and shallow.

Evolutionary roots of excessive anxiety

Brad had every reason to be anxious. But did the intensity of his anxiety fit the reality of his situation? Was his inner voice right that his life was ending, justifying his body’s extreme fight-or-flight response?

A recent book, written by Chris Gilbert, M.D., Ph.D., and me, There’s No Tiger Around That Corner, argues that evolution hardwired our brains to interpret modern challenges to our social status or livelihood as threats to our lives. Citing research from evolutionary psychology, we show that modern brains retain ancient hunter-gatherer survival programs that treat every threat as potentially life-ending.

The reason: Harsh prehistoric environments helped forge our brains into their present forms; most threats could be lethal. Lowered social status could mean expulsion from the clan that kept you alive in dangerous environments. Inability to hunt or gather could lead to starvation. Rustling in the bush could signify a predator about to attack.

Modern brains like Brad’s retain an unconscious bias that transforms unpleasant futures from ones filled with odious skunks into those harboring lethal tigers. Brad did indeed face prolonged unhappiness along with a hit to his social status. But, in contrast to his body’s extreme stress response, he was in no danger of dying.

Reducing excess anxiety using evolutionary psychology

How could Brad dial back his extreme anxiety by transforming his unconscious view of the future from one that’s lethal to one that’s just extremely unpleasant? Chris and I have a simple five-step method that starts by bringing unconscious, primitive beliefs into the cold light of modern reality, where we can critically examine and reframe them.

In Brad’s example, anxiety reduction begins by getting him to acknowledge that his unconscious perceives the looming layoff as an existential threat, prompting him to ask: Is losing my job truly lethal or just extremely bothersome? This question traces extreme anxiety all the way back to its primitive roots, allowing Brad to understand his body’s reaction.

The next step adapts self-talk techniques from cognitive behavioral therapy to persuade the primitive part of Brad’s brain that his life isn’t about to end. Here, instead of supplying the unconscious abstractions such as: “You are misinterpreting unpleasant events as deadly ones," we show anxiety sufferers how to address the primitive part of themselves with vivid, simple language that the primitive brain can understand: For example, "There’s a nasty skunk around the corner, not a tiger.”

The final three steps in our “No Tiger” approach help sufferers navigate the often-difficult path towards lowering anxiety by:

  • Providing realistic views of what to expect on their journey to lower anxiety
  • Describing ways to reward themselves for small victories along the way
  • Outlining techniques that help recovery from normal setbacks.

Chris and I have used these techniques successfully to reduce our own intense anxieties and to help our anxious patients and therapy clients, respectively. If you suffer from intense anxiety, we hope the techniques will also help you. We may not like what lurks around the corner, but letting our primitive brains stress too much about it might do more harm to our well-being than whatever it is that awaits us.

item.title: Art as a Hallmark of Human Consciousness
item.description:
Creativity

Art as a Hallmark of Human Consciousness

Why art may be the strongest evidence of human consciousness.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Consciousness is a subjective experience perceived only by the individual experiencing it.
  • Linguistic symbols are unable to express subjective experiences.
  • An artistic combination of notes, colors, shapes, and words can convey the emotions of artists across time.
  • Can artworks be considered markers of a higher level of consciousness?

Most of us have had a moment when a piece of music, a poem, a movie scene, or a passage from a novel sends chills down our spine. For a few seconds, we feel something powerful, beautiful, and almost impossible to put into words.

Maybe, hundreds of years ago, an artist, at midnight, experienced one of those rare, powerful moments. He reached for a pen and paper to capture what he was feeling before it disappeared. A poem, a melody, a painting, or the first idea for a story was born, and over time, it became a finished work.

Then, years—or even centuries—later, when we encounter that same work, we may find ourselves experiencing a feeling remarkably similar to that of the artist in that midnight moment. We get goosebumps. We are deeply moved. We struggle to explain why. It almost seems as if something hidden between the words, the notes, or the brushstrokes has survived the passage of time, quietly waiting to awaken the same feeling in another mind. Of course, not everyone responds to the same artwork in the same way. It is like a hidden message in the fabric of artwork that is perceived by certain people.

When colloquial language is not enough

Consciousness is defined as the subjective, first-person experience of the world and ourselves. It is a mysterious thing that has been a subject of debate throughout the history of human thought. According to the old scholars, consciousness is related to a metaphysical entity, the soul, whereas modern scientists believe it originates from the brain’s functions, given the prevailing scientific paradigm. However, some philosophers think that it will remain unresolved forever.

One of the characteristics of these first-person experiences is that they cannot be transferred to others by saying. As humans became increasingly social, language evolved into a powerful way to communicate with one another. At first, spoken sounds—and later written symbols—allowed people to share knowledge, coordinate actions, and preserve ideas across generations. As languages grew richer and their vocabularies expanded, they gained a remarkable new capacity. The same words that conveyed facts could also be arranged in ways that expressed love, grief, hope, longing, or awe.

Beyond words, the creative combination of other symbolic forms such as colors, shapes, rhythm, and musical notes gave rise to something even more powerful. Art was no longer just a way to create beauty. It became a way to communicate inner experience, allowing artists to express emotions that are often difficult or even impossible to describe directly. Through a poem, a painting, a symphony, or a novel, one person's private emotional world could be shared with countless others, even across centuries.

Is art unique to humans?

Most philosophers of art hold that art is more than something visually or aesthetically appealing. It involves intention, symbolic meaning, self-awareness, and the deliberate communication of an idea or emotion to an audience that can interpret it. By this definition, there is currently no convincing evidence that any other species creates art in the human sense, using symbols intentionally to represent ideas, express inner experiences, or evoke specific emotional responses in others [1].

Some researchers have suggested that rudimentary forms of art-like behavior exist in other species. Male bowerbirds, for example, build elaborate, colorful structures to attract mates. Yet these displays are generally understood as products of sexual selection rather than symbolic works created to express ideas or emotions. Although many animals produce aesthetically impressive behaviors or objects, there is currently no convincing evidence that any nonhuman species creates art in the human sense, using symbols intentionally to communicate meaning or inner experience. By that definition, art appears to be uniquely human.

However, some researchers argue that artificial intelligence (AI) may one day create poems, music, or paintings that move human audiences just as deeply as human art does. If that happens, would it mean that AI has become conscious and is expressing its own inner experiences through art [2]?

This question lies at the heart of one of the biggest debates in philosophy and cognitive science. Those who view consciousness as an emergent property of a sufficiently complex physical system argue that, in principle, an artificial system with the right architecture might also become conscious. Others disagree. The American philosopher John Searle famously challenged this idea with his Chinese Room thought experiment. He argued that computers manipulate symbols according to rules without understanding what those symbols mean. In his view, even if an AI writes a moving poem or composes beautiful music, that alone does not show that it has subjective experiences or genuine understanding. It may simply be processing patterns rather than expressing emotions it actually feels. This is exactly the gap that matters here: an AI-generated poem may bring us to tears, while the process that produced it never felt a thing [3].

Human artistic works are an effort to convey subjective experience

For centuries, philosophers and scientists have debated consciousness without reaching a consensus. We cannot directly access another person's subjective experience, let alone determine whether an animal or an intelligent machine has one. This is why every proposed marker of consciousness, from the mirror test to Integrated Information Theory and Global Workspace Theory, has remained controversial.

May we have overlooked another possibility? From a behavioristic perspective, perhaps the ability to create original symbolic art that conveys an inner experience to another mind is itself a sign of advanced consciousness. A poem, a painting, or a piece of music is more than a beautiful arrangement of words, colors, or sounds. At its best, it allows one person's subjective experience to be felt by someone else, even centuries later.

If this idea has merit, then humans are still the only species known to possess this ability. Whether another animal—or one day an artificial intelligence—could create art as an expression of its own inner experience, rather than through instinct or predefined rules, remains an open question.

item.title: Resolving the Repetition Compulsion
item.description:
Therapy

Resolving the Repetition Compulsion

How to work through the repetition compulsion in psychotherapy.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • The repetition compulsion is an unconscious recapitulation of the past.
  • Resolving the repetition compulsion requires confronting the past both cognitively and emotionally.
  • Effective therapy involves both cognitive understanding and re-experiencing abandonment feelings.

There are numerous secrets that psychotherapists learn over time about certain commonly occurring symptoms, situations, or patterns of experience and human behavior and what can help to mitigate or alleviate them. One example of this rich clinical wisdom regarding the resolution of such problematical situations pertains to the repetition compulsion as it applies to romantic relationships, as previously discussed in Part 3 of this series

Freud's psychoanalytic couch.
Source: Wikimedia Commons

First Phase of Therapy: Naming or Diagnosing the Problem

During the initial phase of therapy for resolving the repetition compulsion in romantic and other relationships, it is essential to help the patient become cognizant of this pattern in their own life, its consequences, its universality, and, sometimes, to provide a name for it in order to render it more concrete and comprehensible. Hence, cognitively sharing with the patient the concept of a repetition compulsion can be useful in the same way as speaking with them about the phenomena of anxiety or depression can be. Now, the symptom or suffering has a name, can be intellectually understood, and therapeutically confronted. It is no longer something completely unknown, mysterious, or unconscious and can become a meaningful part of the therapeutic conversation.

Middle Phase of Therapy: Working Through

Traditionally, the middle phase of psychodynamic psychotherapy is referred to as the "working through" stage. In addressing the repetition compulsion in therapy, there is sometimes, at some point, an interchange vaguely resembling the scene from the film Good Will Hunting (1997), between the brilliant but physically and emotionally deeply traumatized and consequently pathologically detached patient (Matt Damon) and his psychotherapist (Robin Williams), albeit typically far less intense, cathartic, and dramatic in reality as opposed to the movies. The conversation might go something like this, though it varies significantly from clinician to clinician and with different patients:

This failure is never the child’s fault. Never. Children need and deserve love and acceptance for being who they are, not for their bad behavior. It was not your fault. There was nothing wrong with you. You were just being a kid. You were okay then, and you are okay now.

You were lovable then, and you are still lovable. You were worthy of love then, and you are worthy of love now. Sadly, your parents were not willing or able to provide the love you needed due to their own emotional limitations, despite the fact that they may have, though tragically not in every case, provided for your physical needs for food, shelter, clothing, etc.

The fact is, no parents are perfect, ranging from cruel and incompetent to inept to oblivious to those that are “good enough.” And so we all go through this frustration in one way or another. All parents — like all people — fall short of perfection. Just as our parents did and as parents we inevitably do.

Hearing this potent clinical wisdom at the right time, in the right place, from a person you respect and trust, can be the beginning of a healing process. But, unfortunately, simply reading or being told this, even by an empathic, caring, and authentic therapist, is not enough. If it were, psychotherapy would be unnecessary, or at least a whole lot faster and less arduous. Here is another bit of clinical wisdom: Insight, though absolutely essential, is insufficient. As Otto Rank (1929) once said, at least in some cases, the patient needs not insight or an intellectual explanation of their symptoms but "an emotional experience." However, I would argue that both are necessary and complementary: some explanation and cognitive insight and integration regarding the experience and some experience to underscore and solidify the intellectual or cognitive insight.

Ultimately, the resolution of the repetition compulsion requires re-experiencing and cognitively integrating what Masterson (1990) calls the unconscious "abandonment depression," grief, and rage, which the repetition compulsion defends against feeling. (See my prior post.) Sometimes there is no immediately perceptible response from the person, but other times some teariness may suddenly appear, or it might trigger deeper crying and profound feelings of sadness, relief, anger, and perhaps gratitude or appreciation. As with other things in life, timing is everything. If the person is not ready to hear and receive this powerful message, they will likely fend it off or glibly dismiss it. But this does not necessarily mean that it did not register with the patient—who may need more time to process it emotionally and cognitively and truly come to terms with what was conveyed to them—before being able to consciously acknowledge and accept it. This is one of the inherent limitations of “self-help” literature or relying on the well-intentioned advice of friends, colleagues, or family. It can sometimes point you in the right direction. It can provide valuable illumination, inspiration, and encouragement. But it isn’t a substitute for real psychotherapy.

In any case, this is typically not the end of the neurosis nor of therapy for people but rather the beginning of what is sometimes a long, strenuous, and rocky road toward redeeming and restoring their damaged self-esteem and recognizing that they were not--and are not now--responsible for what happened or did not happen to them as children, nor for the painful failures and shortcomings of their parents or caretakers. This leads us more generally to yet another common existential conundrum clinical wisdom can be helpful in clarifying: What are we responsible for in life and what are we not responsible for? (This key question and what clinical wisdom has to say about it will be addressed in Part 5 of this series.)

Final Phase of Therapy: Resolution, Consolidation, and Termination

Once the working through process has more or less concluded, if all goes well (which is not always the case), therapy enters the final or termination phase of treatment, in which the insights previously gained and transformative emotional experiences had by the patient regarding their own repetition compulsion and its significance and sources are cognitively reviewed, clarified, consolidated, and reconfirmed.

Termination, the end of therapy and loss of the supportive relationship with the clinician, can trigger the old abandonment depression as well as current feelings of fear, anxiety, grief, or rage about this loss of the therapeutic alliance and being on one's own in the world. This serves as a litmus test regarding whether the patient can tolerate and accept intense feelings of despair, hopelessness, anxiety, anger, and abandonment without compulsively reenacting or acting out their repetitive defense mechanism. How the patient (and therapist) deal with these emotions, i.e., defensive avoidance or conscious acceptance, can determine the outcome of treatment, for better or worse. Whether the core neurotic complex of the repetition compulsion has been resolved depends upon the type of relationships the patient is subsequently attracted to and chooses to be involved in either prior to termination of therapy or afterwards, which, in the latter case, remains to be seen.

item.title: What's the Odyssey Really About?
item.description:
Identity

What's the Odyssey Really About?

Why Odysseus' journey is our own.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Homer's epic is about far more than a voyage home.
  • Every adventure tests a different human temptation.
  • This is why the Odyssey still speaks to us.
Home is not merely where we return, but where we are recognised.
Source: Neel Burton. AI generated.

The Odyssey is usually described as the story of a man trying to get home. But this is only the superficial story. The real journey is not geographical but psychological and moral. Odysseus is trying not merely to return to Ithaca, but to become the kind of man who is fit to return.

This is why, after almost three thousand years, the Odyssey continues to speak to us. We are all trying to find our way home—not simply to a place, but to a life that feels genuinely like our own.

Every encounter presents Odysseus with a different temptation. The Lotus-Eaters invite him to forget who he is. Circe seeks to trap him into surrendering his humanity. The Sirens tempt him with endless fascination. Even after escaping the Cyclops Polyphemus, Odysseus succumbs to the temptation of pride. By revealing his name, he forgets his true purpose and risks undoing all that he has achieved. Again and again, Homer asks the same question in different forms: what must we refuse if we are to remain true to ourselves?

The greatest temptation of all comes from Calypso. She offers Odysseus what human beings have always desired: immortality, together with eternal youth and freedom from suffering. Yet he refuses. He chooses instead to return to his ageing wife, his uncertain kingdom, and his mortal life. In doing so, Homer suggests that to become fully human is not to escape our condition, but to embrace it. Only by accepting the limits of human existence can Odysseus finally become himself.

From one perspective, it is a baffling decision. Why exchange paradise for hardship? Like the modern philosopher Bernard Williams, Homer intuits that a life derives its meaning not from its length but from being truly our own. We would rather live a finite life that belongs to us than an endless life that does not.

At last, Odysseus reaches Ithaca. But instead of returning as a conquering hero, he enters his own home disguised as a beggar. His wife does not recognise him. His servants do not recognise him. His kingdom does not recognise him. But one creature does.

Outside the palace gates lies Argos, the hunting dog that Odysseus had raised before leaving for Troy. Once magnificent, Argos has been abandoned on a dung heap to grow old and weak. Yet the moment Odysseus approaches, the dog recognises him. Disguised though he is, stripped of every outward sign of rank and identity, his faithful companion sees through it all. Argos wags his tail, lays back his ears, and, having seen his master one last time, quietly dies. In Homer, recognition has nothing to do with appearances. We are recognised not for what we possess or the roles we play, but for who we truly are.

article continues after advertisement

It is one of the most moving scenes in all of literature because it speaks to one of our deepest longings. We want our lives to amount to something. But we also want to be known and loved for who we are, beneath all our roles, titles, and disguises. Home is not merely where we return. It is where someone knows who we are—and remembers.

Before Odysseus can reclaim his kingdom, he must first reclaim his story. At the court of the Phaeacians, he recounts everything that has happened to him since leaving Troy. By weaving his adventures into a coherent narrative, he recovers not only his past but himself. We make sense of our own lives in much the same way: not merely by living them, but by telling them. There’s a lovely irony here. At the very heart of the Odyssey, Homer hands the poem over to Odysseus himself. Odysseus quite literally rises into the narrator of his own life, before finally heading home.

Perhaps that is why the Odyssey still feels so modern. We, too, leave home, lose our bearings, and become distracted by ambitions, comforts, fears, and false identities. We, too, sometimes wonder how we ended up living the lives we are living.

The Odyssey endures because Homer understood that the longest journey any of us will ever undertake is not outward across the seas, but inward into our hearts.

Neel Burton is author of The Meaning of Myth.

item.title: How the Invisible String Theory Might Affect Your Dating
item.description:
Mating

How the Invisible String Theory Might Affect Your Dating

Believing in destiny can be your friend or foe in romance.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • The invisible string theory is the belief that an unseen "string" connects you to someone somewhere.
  • The belief, then, is that over time and space, this string will eventually pull the two of you to be together.
  • Believing this can help you get through tough times in your dating journey and help you be more relaxed.
  • However, don't let this belief give away too much agency in your life and keep you with the wrong person.
The "Invisible String Theory" is the belief that an unseen "string" connects you to someone somewhere.
Source: Master1305/Shutterstcok

You could say that this so-called “invisible string theory” has become quite visible on social media. A seemingly obvious question, though, is whether influencers advancing this theory have much science to back it up or are—you know—just stringing you along. However, believe it or not, whether this theory is actually true may not really matter if you use it to string together the right approach to dating.

What Is the “Invisible String Theory”

The invisible string theory is the belief that you are somehow connected to someone else somewhere in the world through some kind of an unseen “string.” And that over time and space, this string or force will eventually pull the two of you to be together—regardless of what may seemingly stand in the way. In other words, you are destined to be with this person.

Consider this a variation of the you’re-meant-to-be-with-a-particular-person and everything-happens-for-a-reason beliefs that emerged long before the days of social media influencers. The origins trace back to ancient Chinese folklore’s “Red Thread of Fate”—an invisible, unbreakable red cord that supposedly ties together those destined to meet, love, or help each other in some way.

Such a string has run through recent pop culture too. It was basically the entire plotline of the How I Met Your Mother TV series, which strung together a series of seemingly random events that led the protagonist, Ted Mosby, to meet the eventual mother of his children, Tracy McConnell—hence the name of the show. It was the topic of that Taylor Swift song, “Invisible String,” too. And if Taylor Swift sings it, then it’s gotta hold, right?

It Is Hard to Prove or Completely Refute the Invisible String Theory

Well, not exactly. This invisible string theory ain’t about physics and doesn’t have much solid scientific evidence behind it. Instead, it is part of the continuing debate over how random versus pre-determined the universe and its events are. If you could somehow provide a definitive scientific answer to end this debate, then you could find yourself winning the Nobel Prize and practically every scientific award out there—assuming, of course, that you are meant to win those awards.

The evidence that people often provide for the invisible string theory is largely anecdotal. For example, a happily married couple may recount all the conditions and events that had to be in place for them to meet as “proof” that their union was meant to be. However, no one knows what the counterfactual may have been—namely, if something had been different along the way, would they still have ended up together again regardless? Moreover, recall biases can be at play—people selectively recalling “signs” that they were destined to be together while overlooking similar signs being present for other people around them as well. Furthermore, humans often ascribe patterns and meanings to situations even when none are present.

article continues after advertisement

Therefore, consider the invisible string theory to be less a scientific theory and more a spiritual belief or approach to life. You can’t really prove or refute it. That doesn’t make it inherently good or bad, though, or useless.

How the Invisible String Theory Could Help Your Dating Life

No, any “don’t stop believing” thing could keep you hopeful on your dating journey even when going through a string of frustrations. It could help you cast all those bad dating and relationship experiences as needed preparation to do the right things once that right partner finally arrives. And a more optimistic outlook in itself can help you keep trying, be more open to possibilities, and even appear more attractive. Believing that destiny is somehow helping you along could take pressure off your dating as well—so that you obsess less over what you say or do during a particular date and instead feel more relaxed and freer to be your authentic self.

Moreover, it could help you untangle yourself from the wrong relationships and raise your standards appropriately. The steadfast belief that someone better might come along can give you the courage to drop someone who is not treating you right. It can also help you even embrace, gasp, singlehood.

How the Invisible String Theory Could Hurt Your Dating Life

On the other end of the string, if you mistakenly believe that you were meant to be with someone who is wrong for you, then such a belief could further entangle your situation. You might overlook bad behaviors, clear incompatibilities, or signs that the other person doesn’t really want to be with you simply because that whole destiny thing wants you two to be together.

Relying a little too much on destiny can give away your agency in life, so that you don’t make enough effort to make things go the way you want to go. In other words, don’t stop trying to improve yourself and your situation and expect the right person to somehow magically end up in your lap or wherever else you want that person to be.

Another concern is that this theory might raise your expectations way too high. In How I Met Your Mother, the character Klaus defined for Ted one fictional German word, Lebenslangerschicksalsschatz, as your “lifelong treasure of destiny”—implying that you should look for the person who is your instant, perfect match rather than settling for a Beinaheleidenschaftsgegenstand, another fictional German term, which Klaus defined as “The thing that is almost the thing that you want... but it is not quite.”

article continues after advertisement

Ach je! The concern then is Beinaheleidenschaftsgegenstand-ing anyone once you find anything that doesn’t match your expectations exactly. This would overlook the fact that lifelong partnerships are never perfect and require hard work and dedication to overcome any differences.

Finally, even if you believe in the invisible string theory, don’t obsess about it, letting it dictate everything. Part of enjoying life is accepting all its uncertainties and simply experiencing what happens to come your way rather than always having to string together a theory to explain why.

item.title: 2 ‘Messy Habits’ That Instantly Boost Your Productivity
item.description:
Zeigarnik Effect

2 ‘Messy Habits’ That Instantly Boost Your Productivity

Some habits look disorganized from the outside but make you more productive.

Posted July 31, 2026

Source: Cottonbro Studio / Pexels

In the 1920s, a Berlin psychologist named Bluma Zeigarnik noticed something odd about the waiters at a local café, according to a 2020 study published in Memory and Cognition that traces the discovery back to its origin. They could, seemingly out of habit, recite a long, complicated, unpaid order from memory with total precision, then lose every detail of it the moment the bill was settled.

The finding launched decades of research into why unfinished business seems to hang onto the mind more insistently than finished business does. That question, it turns out, is more complicated than it first appeared. It also points to something worth taking seriously about how sustained, high-quality work actually gets done: two of the most reliable habits behind it are never finished-looking.

Neither habit favors chaos. However, both refuse to manufacture order—before order has actually been earned. This turns out to be harder and more useful than it sounds.

Habit 1: Leaving Work Visibly Unfinished

What Zeigarnik documented in waiters extends directly to the work desk. An open draft, a half-built spreadsheet, a slide deck saved mid-thought instead of neatly closed out: these are all examples of what psychologists call the Zeigarnik effect, and the mechanism is straightforward. An unresolved task stays cognitively “live.” A 2025 study published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications found some evidence people remember unfinished work better, but confirmed a real, durable tendency to pick it back up. This is the kind of readiness that a completed task immediately loses. That readiness is what makes it possible to sit back down at a project hours or days later without paying the full cost of reconstructing where things stood.

Wrapping a task up neatly, purely for the satisfaction of calling it done, can flatten the tension that would have carried the next good idea forward. The habit stops paying off, of course, when the open loop becomes a source of dread rather than a placeholder. There’s a meaningful difference between deliberately leaving something unfinished and anxiously avoiding it, and only the latter is doing useful cognitive work.

Habit 2: Letting Your Workspace Fall Into Disorder

Efficiency culture treats a tidy desk as a proxy for a tidy mind, but the psychologist Kathleen Vohs complicated that assumption in a now well-known line of research. She and her colleagues found that people working in visibly disordered rooms generated more original, less conventional ideas than people working in orderly ones, according to a 2013 study published in Psychological Science. Having said that, a 2019 study published in Frontiers in Psychology that attempted to replicate the finding came up empty; it’s best read as suggestive rather than settled. The orderly room participants weren’t just more conventional; they were more generous and more likely to choose the healthy snack. Order didn’t make them happier workers; it made them more cautious ones.

The likely explanation is that a disordered environment loosens the mind’s grip on convention. Tidy, symmetrical spaces seem to cue rule-following; looser ones seem to cue exploration. That distinction matters more than it might first appear. For work that demands precision, like reconciling numbers or proofreading a contract, order still earns its keep. For generative work, disorder seems to buy something order can’t: a wider space of possible answers, rather than a fast retreat to the first respectable one.

How These 2 Habits Work Together

Both habits are, underneath, a form of comfort with unresolved ambiguity. The psychologist Arie Kruglanski built an entire body of research around a related trait he called the need for closure, as a 2015 review published in Advances in Experimental Social Psychology lays out: the urge to settle on an answer, any answer, to stop sitting with uncertainty. A high need for closure feels productive in the moment. It rarely produces the best available, since it favors the first tidy one instead.

People who leave tasks open and desks a little disordered are, often without naming it this way, tolerating more ambiguity for longer than convention recommends. That tolerance is uncomfortable, which is exactly why productivity advice keeps pushing in the opposite direction.

It’s also, on the evidence, where the better ideas and the smoother returns to interrupted work tend to come from. The reverse is worth noticing too: someone who clears every task and every surface before allowing themselves a break isn’t necessarily more disciplined. They may have less patience for the discomfort of a loose end, even in the moments when a little more of that discomfort would have served them.

None of this recommends chaos as a strategy. It recommends suspicion toward the urge to clean up too soon, on the desk or on the screen, before the mess has finished being useful.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: How Your Guilt Is Feeding Your Adult Child’s Shame
item.description:
Parenting

How Your Guilt Is Feeding Your Adult Child’s Shame

The parenting instinct that's quietly making the struggle worse.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Guilt is conveyed between parent and adult child before a single word is spoken.
  • Guilt drives parental rescue, and rescue confirms the adult child's shame.
  • Breaking the loop starts with a parent regulating their own guilt, not their child's behavior.

Recently, Judy* (name changed for privacy), a coaching client of mine, said, “Dr. Jeff, I feel like crap for all the things I wish I could have done better for Billy (her 29-year-old son). The divorce when he was just 7 years old, not getting him diagnosed with ADHD until almost the end of high school, and then the comments I made about his choice of friends and his smoking weed. I don’t know, it’s like I feel bad, then I bend over backward to help him, and he treats me like crap, and we are both caught up in this guilt-blame-shame cycle.”

I’m often surprised by how many parents I coach assume their guilt should be obligatory. It is almost as if they see it as an internal, emotionally draining, private tax they dutifully pay for loving imperfectly. But their guilt is rarely private. It leaks into tone, timing, and the eyes of the parent paying it, and a struggling adult child is exquisitely tuned to read exactly that leak. Let’s look at how a parent’s guilt quietly becomes their adult child’s shame in three ways.

1. Guilt broadcasts before a single word is spoken.

Shame in struggling adult children runs on a specific signal: “Something is wrong with me.” An adult child picks up that signal not from criticism, but from a parent’s anxious over-concern. Just reflect for a minute on the impact of that extra-careful tone, your hovering check-ins, your wince or swallow, or quavering voice before a hard conversation. To the parent, this reads as, “You know we love you and want the best for you,” cushioned by remorse over past mistakes.

To the adult child, it reads as confirmation that “I am the family screw-up and the problem they need to be constantly managing.” It gets even more problematic because guilt, delivered as gentleness, conveys “you’re fragile.” In the words of one adult child I recently spoke with, “It’s like I’m stuck feeling all this big-time shame, yet it doesn’t help that they see me as a glass object that can break at any time.”

2. Guilt drives rescue, and rescue confirms the shame.

A guilty parent tends to jump into their first-responder uniform (or SWAT team leader vest and gear) to overcorrect, give more money, offer more advice, or try to make a quiet intervention behind the scenes. For such parents, it’s a way of settling their own conscience, not necessarily because the adult child asked. Each rescue, however loving and well-intended, carries an unspoken verdict: “I don’t trust you to handle this.”

The adult child absorbs that “I’m totally incompetent” verdict faster than any spoken reassurance can undo it. This is how the overthinking loop locks in: parents’ guilt produces rescue, rescue produces dependence, dependence produces more shame, more shame produces behavior that triggers more parental guilt. Sure, nobody planned this, but everybody’s stuck in it.

3. Breaking the loop starts with regulating your own guilt, not your child’s behavior.

This is the exact mechanism I dig into in my book You Ruined My Life. It’s the premise that connection with your child, at any age, isn’t built by managing their struggle for them, but by managing your own reaction to it first. Please don’t hear me as saying the fix isn’t colder parenting. Rather, it’s a parent who processes their guilt before it reaches their child, not through them.

That might mean naming it to a therapist, a partner, or a journal, rather than to a 27-year-old who’s already drowning in self-judgment. What the adult child actually needs isn’t a parent who feels bad on their behalf. It’s a parent who can look steady, even hopeful, as the struggle remains unresolved. Calm confidence, not anxious atonement, is what finally gives an adult child room to believe they’re capable rather than being carried.

The takeaway

Your guilt was never yours to hand to your adult child. Seeing your child’s grit and successes amid their struggles will help you let go of your guilt.
